subject: ela
intro: Read each transcript of a speaker's remarks as if you were hearing the speaker. Then evaluate the spoken argument by identifying the speaker's claims, separating claims from reasons and evidence, and judging whether each claim is supported.

items.prompt:
A student gave this short speech to the class: "I think our school should start a recycling club. Right now we throw away hundreds of paper sheets every week, and all of it ends up in the trash. A recycling club could collect that paper and send it to be reused. Last year, the club at Lincoln Middle School recycled over two thousand pounds of paper. We can do the same thing here if we just get organized. A recycling club would make our school cleaner and help the planet."

What is the speaker's main argument?
A) Lincoln Middle School recycled over two thousand pounds of paper.
B) Our school should start a recycling club.
C) The school throws away hundreds of paper sheets every week.
D) Recycling is a topic many students care about.
items.answer: B) Our school should start a recycling club.

steps: The main argument is the position the speaker wants the audience to accept, not just the topic.
The speaker opens and closes by urging the school to start a recycling club, so B states that position.
A is a piece of evidence the speaker gives, not the overall argument.
C is a supporting fact, not the position the speaker is arguing for.
D names the topic in a general way instead of the specific position the speaker takes, a common mix-up between topic and argument.

items.prompt:
During morning announcements, a speaker said: "Students should bring reusable water bottles to school. Our cafeteria sells about three hundred plastic bottles every single day, and most of them get thrown out by lunchtime. A reusable bottle can be refilled at the new fountains in every hallway. Bringing your own bottle is an easy way to cut down on all that plastic waste."

Which statement is a piece of evidence the speaker gives to support the argument?
A) Students should bring reusable water bottles to school.
B) Bringing your own bottle is an easy way to cut down on plastic waste.
C) The cafeteria sells about three hundred plastic bottles every single day.
D) Reusable bottles are better for the environment.
items.answer: C) The cafeteria sells about three hundred plastic bottles every single day.

steps: Evidence is a concrete fact, number, or example the speaker cites to back up the argument.
C gives a specific number (about three hundred bottles a day), which is concrete evidence.
A is the speaker's claim or position, not evidence.
B is a general statement of the speaker's point, not a concrete fact.
D is an opinion the speaker did not actually state as proof, so it is not the evidence given.

items.prompt:
A speaker told the class: "Our field trip should go to the science museum. The museum has a new space exhibit that connects to the unit we just finished on planets. Admission is free for school groups, so the trip would not cost anyone money. The museum is only a short bus ride away, so we would have plenty of time to explore."

The speaker claims the trip would not cost anyone money. Which statement does the speaker use to support that claim?
A) The museum has a new space exhibit about planets.
B) Admission is free for school groups.
C) The museum is only a short bus ride away.
D) The field trip should go to the science museum.
items.answer: B) Admission is free for school groups.

steps: The question asks for the support tied to one specific claim: that the trip would not cost money.
B directly explains why there is no cost (admission is free for school groups), so it supports that claim.
A supports a different claim, that the trip connects to what the class studied.
C supports a different claim, that there would be enough time.
D is the speaker's overall position, not support for the cost claim.

items.prompt:
A student gave this speech in a debate: "Our town needs a later start time for middle school. First, doctors who study sleep say that students this age need about nine hours of rest, and a 7:15 start makes that almost impossible for kids who ride the early bus. Researchers at one university tracked two schools and found that the school with a later start had fewer students falling asleep in class. Also, a later start would just be better for everyone, trust me. We all know mornings are hard. So please support a later bell."

Which claim does the speaker make WITHOUT backing it up with reasons or evidence?
A) A later start would just be better for everyone.
B) Students this age need about nine hours of rest.
C) A 7:15 start makes enough sleep almost impossible for early-bus riders.
D) One school with a later start had fewer students falling asleep in class.
items.answer: A) A later start would just be better for everyone.

steps: An unsupported claim rests on opinion or assertion with no reasons or evidence behind it.
A is followed only by "trust me" and "we all know mornings are hard," which is opinion and feeling, not proof, so A is unsupported.
B is supported by sleep doctors the speaker cites.
C is supported by the point about the early bus and the nine-hour need.
D is supported by the university researchers who tracked two schools. A common error is assuming a confidently stated claim must be supported, but A offers no real evidence.

items.prompt:
A speaker argued: "The school library should stay open after the last bell. Many students cannot get help at home, so an open library gives them a quiet place to do homework. In a survey our class took, forty-two out of sixty students said they would use an after-school library at least twice a week. Keeping it open would not require new staff, because a teacher has already offered to supervise. An open library would help everyone succeed."

Which part of the speaker's argument is evidence, NOT a claim?
A) The school library should stay open after the last bell.
B) An open library gives students a quiet place to do homework.
C) Forty-two out of sixty students said they would use an after-school library at least twice a week.
D) An open library would help everyone succeed.
items.answer: C) Forty-two out of sixty students said they would use an after-school library at least twice a week.

steps: Evidence is concrete data or facts; a claim is a statement the speaker wants the listener to accept.
C reports specific survey data (forty-two out of sixty students), which is evidence.
A is the speaker's main claim or position.
B is a claim about what the library would do for students.
D is a broad claim, not concrete proof. Treating a claim as if it were the evidence is a common mix-up the data in C avoids.

items.prompt:
A student presented this oral report: "We should add more bike racks at the front of the school. Every morning I see bikes leaning against the fence and the wall because the two racks we have are completely full by 8 a.m. Last week the principal counted forty-one bikes and only twenty rack spaces. More racks would also keep the bikes from blocking the doorway, which is a safety problem the custodian mentioned. Adding racks is cheap and easy, so there is no reason not to."

The speaker claims that the current racks are not enough. Which support does the speaker give for THAT specific claim?
A) Adding racks is cheap and easy.
B) Bikes blocking the doorway is a safety problem the custodian mentioned.
C) The principal counted forty-one bikes and only twenty rack spaces.
D) We should add more bike racks at the front of the school.
items.answer: C) The principal counted forty-one bikes and only twenty rack spaces.

steps: The question asks for support of one claim: the current racks are not enough.
C gives the count showing forty-one bikes but only twenty spaces, which directly proves the racks cannot hold all the bikes.
A supports a different point, that adding racks is easy to do.
B supports a different claim about safety at the doorway.
D is the speaker's overall position, not evidence for the shortage. Picking a true but unrelated detail is a common matching error C avoids.

items.prompt:
A student gave this speech to the student council: "Our cafeteria should bring back the salad bar, and honestly anyone who disagrees just does not care about students' health. Here is why it matters. When the salad bar was open two years ago, the cafeteria's own records showed that about ninety students used it each day, so there is clearly real demand. A salad bar also adds fresh vegetables to lunch, and the school nurse has said that more students should be eating vegetables. Some people will say it costs too much, but that is just an excuse from people who would rather complain than help. A salad bar is the obvious right choice, and only someone who ignores the facts would say no."

The speaker insists the cafeteria should bring back the salad bar. Which part of this argument is an unsupported move rather than real evidence?
A) The cafeteria's records showed about ninety students used the salad bar each day.
B) The school nurse said more students should be eating vegetables.
C) Anyone who disagrees just does not care about students' health.
D) The salad bar adds fresh vegetables to lunch.
items.answer: C) Anyone who disagrees just does not care about students' health.

steps: An unsupported move uses loaded wording or attacks opponents instead of offering reasons and evidence.
C attacks anyone who disagrees by saying they do not care about students, which is biased, emotional language, not proof, so it is the unsupported move.
A is real evidence: a specific count from the cafeteria's records.
B is support drawn from the school nurse, a relevant source.
D is a reasonable claim about what the salad bar provides. Counting persuasive or loaded wording as if it were evidence is the trap C represents.

items.prompt:
Two students debated whether the school should require uniforms. Maria said: "Uniforms would reduce distractions. At a nearby school that switched to uniforms, the office reported that dress-code arguments dropped by half in one year, which gave teachers more class time. Uniforms also cost families less over time, because a survey of parents found most spent less on clothes after the switch." Then Jordan answered: "Uniforms are a terrible idea. Everyone I have ever talked to hates them, and besides, my older cousin wore a uniform and said it was awful. Uniforms just crush who you are. We are individuals, and that is the end of the discussion."

Whose argument is better supported, and why?
A) Jordan's, because Jordan spoke with strong feeling and sounded very sure.
B) Maria's, because she backs her claims with a reported statistic and a parent survey, while Jordan offers mainly opinion and one personal story.
C) Jordan's, because talking to many people and a relative's experience prove uniforms are bad.
D) Maria's, because she spoke for a longer time than Jordan did.
items.answer: B) Maria's, because she backs her claims with a reported statistic and a parent survey, while Jordan offers mainly opinion and one personal story.

steps: A better-supported argument relies on relevant evidence, not just feeling or a single anecdote.
Maria cites a reported statistic (arguments dropped by half) and a parent survey, which are concrete and relevant, so B correctly explains why her case is stronger.
A judges Jordan's argument by how sure he sounded, but confidence is not evidence.
C treats "everyone I talked to" and one cousin's experience as proof, but these are opinion and a single anecdote, not sufficient evidence.
D judges support by how long Maria spoke, but length is not the same as relevant or sufficient evidence.
